title: Quorums (N, R, W)
subtitle: Watch a leaderless database write to three copies, survive a dead node, and heal itself afterwards.
learn: What N, R and W mean and why R + W > N makes reads overlap with the latest write
Why a leaderless system can keep accepting writes while a replica is down
How a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff trade guarantees for availability
How read repair and anti-entropy bring stale replicas back in sync
What quorums still do not give you, such as ordering of concurrent writes

steps.title: No leader, so who is right?
steps.body: In a leaderless database (the original Amazon Dynamo design, Cassandra, Riak), any node can accept a write. Each key is stored on N replicas, meaning N copies on different machines. Here N = 3: replicas A, B and C. Replicas fail and come back at different times, so their copies drift apart. If a client reads while they disagree, how many replicas must it ask to be sure it sees the latest write?
steps.idea: With no single leader, correctness comes from how many replicas you wait for, not from asking one special node.
steps.caption: One key lives on three replicas. Any of them may be behind.

steps.title: Write with W = 2
steps.body: The client sends cart:42 = v2 (version 2 of a shopping cart) to a coordinator, the node that runs the request. Any node can play this role; it is drawn separately here. The coordinator forwards the write to all three replicas but waits for only W = 2 acknowledgements (acks, meaning "got it" replies). A and B answer in about 2 ms. C is down and never answers. Two acks meet W, so the write succeeds and C is simply behind for now.
steps.idea: A write succeeds once W replicas have it. The other N - W copies catch up later.
steps.caption: A and B ack; C is down. Two acks meet W = 2.

steps.title: Read with R = 2
steps.body: C has restarted but still holds the old v1. Now the client reads. The coordinator asks R = 2 replicas for their copy, say B and C. B returns v2 and C returns v1, so the coordinator picks the newest, v2, and replies. (It compares version numbers or timestamps; the clocks lesson covers why that is harder than it sounds.) Why is the answer always fresh? Any 2 replicas must include at least one that took the write, because 2 + 2 = 4 is greater than N = 3. Read repair, which would also fix C, comes later.
steps.idea: If R + W > N, every read set shares at least one replica with every write set, so a read sees the latest write that finished before it began. This is not full linearizability (see the CAP and consensus lessons).
steps.caption: Read set {B, C} overlaps write set {A, B} at B.

steps.title: Turning the knobs
steps.body: In Cassandra and Riak you can choose R and W per request. W = 1 with R = 1 is the fastest, but 1 + 1 is not greater than 3, so a read can hit a stale replica. The animation shows this: after the W = 2 write, R = 1 happens to ask C and returns v1, because 1 + 2 is not greater than 3. W = 3 with R = 1 gives fresh reads, but one dead replica then blocks every write. The common middle for N = 3 is W = 2, R = 2, which survives one failure on both paths. Bigger quorums also wait on slower replicas, which raises tail latency (the speed of the slowest few percent of requests).
steps.idea: Pick R and W to trade freshness, write availability and latency. R + W > N buys overlap, at the cost of waiting for more nodes.
steps.caption: R = 1 asked only the stale replica C and got v1.

steps.title: Too many replicas down
steps.body: Now a network problem cuts the coordinator off from A and C. Only B is reachable, and W is still 2. A strict quorum would reject the write, since only 1 of the 3 designated replicas can ack. A sloppy quorum is more flexible. The coordinator writes to a healthy node outside the set, D, tagged with a hint: "this data belongs to C". B plus D give two acks, so the write is accepted. Dynamo and Riak count stand-ins toward the quorum. Cassandra stores hints but does not count them toward the consistency level (except level ANY).
steps.idea: A sloppy quorum keeps writes available during failures by counting stand-in nodes, at the cost of the overlap guarantee.
steps.caption: D holds C's copy as a hint so the write can succeed.

steps.title: The catch with sloppy quorums
steps.body: Here is the catch. D is not one of the three replicas that reads consult. While the partition lasts, another client reaches a second coordinator on A and C's side (drawn as the same Coordinator box to keep the diagram small). It reads A and C, and both missed v3: A returns v2 and C returns v1. It answers v2, even though v3 was acknowledged and R + W is still greater than N. Only 1 of the 3 designated replicas (B) holds v3. The overlap promise only works when the quorums are drawn from the designated replicas. Sloppy quorums give eventual consistency and high write availability, not a read-your-writes guarantee.
steps.idea: With stand-ins, R + W > N no longer guarantees a fresh read until the hint is delivered.
steps.caption: Reading A and C returns old data; v3 sits on B and D.

steps.title: Hinted handoff
steps.body: The partition heals and C is reachable again. D notices it holds a hint for C, forwards v3 to it, then deletes its temporary copy. This is hinted handoff: a stand-in holds a write for someone who is away and hands it over on return. Systems usually cap how long they keep hints, often a few hours, so a node that stays down longer must be repaired another way. Handoff is a fast path, not a guarantee.
steps.idea: Hinted handoff replays missed writes to a recovered replica, but hints are best-effort and time-limited.
steps.caption: D hands v3 to C once C is back.

steps.title: Read repair
steps.body: A is still on v2, because it was cut off during the v3 write. In this example no hint was stored for A (D was the only stand-in and it holds C's hint; hints for A could also have been lost or expired). A client now reads from A and B. B returns v3 and A returns v2. The coordinator answers the client with v3 and, at the same moment, writes v3 back to A. The read itself found the gap and fixed it, at the cost of one extra write. This is read repair.
steps.idea: Read repair heals stale replicas as a side effect of reads, so popular keys converge quickly.
steps.caption: The coordinator sees that A is behind and pushes v3 to it.

steps.title: Background anti-entropy
steps.body: Read repair only fixes keys that get read, and hints can expire or be lost. So replicas also compare their data in the background (in some systems this is a scheduled repair job). Each builds a Merkle tree, a tree of hashes over key ranges, and sends its root hash to a peer. If the roots match, nothing is copied. If not, they walk down to the ranges that differ and exchange only those keys. Example: a rarely read key in range 7 was missed by both hints and reads, so A is behind on range 7 and B sends A those keys. Cassandra's nodetool repair builds Merkle trees on demand; Dynamo and Riak run anti-entropy automatically.
steps.idea: Anti-entropy uses hash trees to find and fix differences cheaply, covering keys that read repair and hints miss.
steps.caption: A and B compare hash roots, then sync only the differing range.

steps.title: What quorums give you
steps.body: Store N copies. Wait for W acks on writes and R replies on reads. If R + W > N and you use the real replica set, every read overlaps the latest write. Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff favour availability. Read repair and anti-entropy pull stale copies back in line. Quorums do not order concurrent writes to the same key: that needs version tracking, covered in the clocks lesson.
steps.idea: Quorums tune freshness versus availability. Healing mechanisms bring the copies together eventually.
steps.caption: Write to W, read from R, repair in the background.

quiz.q: Which setting does NOT guarantee that a read overlaps with the most recent acknowledged write (assume strict quorums and no failures during the read)?
quiz.why: Overlap needs R + W > N. For N = 5, W = 2 and R = 3 give 5, which is not greater than 5, so a read set of 3 can miss both replicas that took the write.

quiz.q: A sloppy quorum accepts a write using a stand-in node outside the key's usual N replicas. Why can a later read with R + W > N still return old data?
options: The read set may contain only designated replicas that never received the write, since the stand-in is not among them
R + W > N only applies to leader-based systems
Hinted handoff deletes the data after a write
quiz.why: The overlap argument depends on both sets being drawn from the same N replicas. The acknowledged copy lives on a node reads do not consult until the hint is handed off.

quiz.q: A rarely accessed key is stale on one replica, the hint meant for it expired, and nobody reads the key. What eventually repairs it?
options: Read repair, because every key is read eventually
Anti-entropy, which compares replicas in the background using hash trees
quiz.why: Read repair needs a read and the hint is gone, so a periodic background comparison such as Merkle-tree anti-entropy is what finds and copies the missing data.

quiz.q: You set N = 3 and W = 3 to make writes as durable as possible. What is the main cost?
options: If any one replica is down or slow, writes fail or stall
Reads can no longer see the latest write
The coordinator must be a leader
quiz.why: W = N means every replica must acknowledge, so a single failure blocks writes and the slowest replica sets write latency. Durability goes up but availability goes down.

cheatsheet.def: N = replicas per key, W = acks required before a write succeeds, R = replies required before a read returns. In systems like Cassandra and Riak, R and W can be chosen per request.

Read and write sets share a replica, so a read sees the latest completed write. A write that fails to reach W acks is not rolled back, so a later read may still see it. Not linearizability. Common for N = 3: R = W = 2.
floor(N/2) + 1 replicas, for example 2 of 3 or 3 of 5. Using it for both R and W tolerates the loss of a minority.
Accepts writes on stand-in nodes outside the key's replica set when designated ones are unreachable. More available, but loses the overlap guarantee.
A stand-in stores the write with a hint naming the intended replica and forwards it when that node returns. Hints are time-limited and best-effort.
When a read sees different versions, the coordinator returns the newest and writes it back to stale replicas. Only fixes keys that are read.
Background sync where replicas compare Merkle trees of their data and copy only the differing ranges. Catches cold keys and expired hints.
They do not order concurrent writes to the same key. You still need version metadata such as vector clocks or a merge rule to avoid silently losing updates.
